Jean Renoir. A French master filmmaker of the nineteen-thirties to nineteen-sixties, the son of Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, who synthesised realism, humanism, and visual poetry into films of extraordinary warmth and social insight. His masterpieces Grand Illusion and The Rules of the Game stand as two of cinema's greatest achievements, balancing popular narrative with formal sophistication.

He made Grand Illusion in 1937, an anti-war film about escaped prisoners of war that transcends national boundaries through acts of human sympathy and music. He created The Rules of the Game in 1939, widely considered one of cinema's supreme works—a sprawling ensemble piece capturing French society on the eve of war. Renoir pioneered deep focus and moving camera, using the full spatial depth of the frame to orchestrate human action rather than relying on cuts.

He is known for generosity toward his actors. His films are distinguished by performances of rare authenticity and empathy. He spent the war years in America, where he continued directing before returning to France to reestablish his legacy. He adapted texts including The Lower Depths and Toni, bringing literary and theatrical sensibility into cinema. His influence spans generations. He is sometimes called cinema's greatest humanist for his refusal to sentimentalise or judge his characters.

Robert Bresson was a contemporary who shared Renoir's humanist concerns but diverged into ascetic formalism. Jacques Demy was a later director who inherited Renoir's poetic approach to realism and colour. His father was Pierre-Auguste Renoir, the Impressionist painter, and visual sensibility flows from that tradition. Grand Illusion remains his definitive anti-war statement.
